newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan nuclear industry sees no need for review.
newsitem.headline: Japan nuclear industry sees no need for review.

text.p: An accident involving radiation contamination of workers at Japan's only nuclear reprocessing plant is no reason to review the country's overall atomic energy plans, officials said on Thursday.
The officials also said the accident would not upset power utilities' reprocessing programmes or lead to an increase in nuclear waste currently sent overseas, mainly to France.

The accident on Tuesday in which 35 workers suffered tiny amounts of radiation contamination set off speculation about the possibility of a review of an industry already reeling from an accident and a cover-up attempt at the Monju prototype fast-breeder reactor in December 1995.

The Tokaimura reprocessing plant is a crucial unit of natural-resource-poor Japan's attempt to boost energy self-sufficiency by establishing its own nuclear fuel cycle. The cycle refers to the process in which uranium is refined, used as fuel, and the spent fuel reprocessed.

The Monju reactor and the reprocessing plant are both operated by the state-run Power Reactor and Nuclear Fuel Development Corporation (PNC). Monju can be fuelled by plutonium recovered from spent fuel.

Tuesday's accident occurred when a fire which caused radiation to escape was not extinguished properly and caused an explosion hours later. Some radiation leaked from the plant, but at levels far below those that would pose health risks to the public, a PNC spokesman said.

The complex at Tokaimura, 160 km (100 miles) northeast of Tokyo, handles only about 12 percent of spent nuclear fuel from Japan's 50 running commercial nuclear power plants. The bulk is reprocessed either in France or Britain.

"We do not believe that Japanese utility companies will change their reprocessing contracts with overseas operators because of the recent accident," a Federation of Electric Power Companies spokesman said.

Japan is in the process of building a second plant capable of handling 800 tU (uranium tonne), or a large majority of the roughly 900 tU of spent fuel that is produced every year by Japan's nuclear power plants.

Any change in the plan to build the complex -- which is due to begin operating only some time after 2003 -- would have serious consequences on the utilities reprocessing programme, industry sources said.

A Ministry of International Trade and Industry (MITI) official said the government remained committed to its nuclear programme. The second reprocessing facility applied a different technology, and there was no need to review plans there, he said.

Japan's power industry has altogether contracted to consign about 7,100 tU of spent fuel for reprocessing overseas, the power federation said. About 6,790 tU of the contracted volume has already been shipped overseas as of last December.
The secretary-general of the Citizens Nuclear Information Centre, Hideyuki Ban, said he expected the latest accident to have a significant psychological impact on the general public.
"I think the (accident) is going to provide momentum to people calling for an end to Japan's plutonium energy policy," he said.
He noted that the power industry had already been forced to make a review of its policy after the accident at Monju, which remains closed.

He gave as examples the referendum in the small northern town of Maki last August on Tohoku Electric Power Company's plan to build a nuclear power plant. Voters returned a majority "no" vote in the non-binding poll.
On Tuesday, Kyushu Electric Power, one of Japan's 10 power companies, said it had abandoned a plan to build a nuclear plant in southern Japan because of strong local opposition.
